resources.string: Lateral nasal wall
Side cutaway of the nasal cavity with the septum removed
Nasal vestibule
The vestibule sits just inside the nostril. Its skin-like lining contains coarse hairs that catch some larger particles.
Superior nasal concha
The smallest of the three usual conchae projects from the upper back part of the lateral wall. Part of its surface lies in the olfactory region.
Middle nasal concha
This curved shelf is part of the ethmoid bone. The passage beneath it receives drainage from several of the paranasal sinuses.
Inferior nasal concha
The largest and lowest concha is a separate bone. Its lining helps warm and humidify passing air; the tear duct opens into the passage below it.
Choana
Each side of the nasal cavity has a posterior opening called a choana. It leads into the nasopharynx above the soft palate.
Pharyngeal regions
Sagittal section through the three regions of the pharynx
Nasopharynx
The upper pharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. It carries air from the nose into the throat.
Oropharynx
The middle pharynx lies behind the mouth and tongue, below the soft palate. Both air and swallowed material pass through it.
Laryngopharynx
The lowest region lies behind the larynx. It continues downward into the esophagus, while the laryngeal inlet opens toward the front.
Soft palate
This movable extension behind the hard palate lifts during swallowing, separating the nasopharynx from the passage below.
Epiglottis
This leaf-shaped cartilage stands near the entrance to the larynx. During swallowing it folds back over the inlet, helping protect the airway.
Inferior surface
Diaphragm from below, with the front at the top
Central tendon
The pale, three-lobed sheet lies where the surrounding diaphragm muscle fibers converge. It moves with the muscle during breathing.
Costal muscle
Fibers attach along the inside of the lower ribs and their cartilages and run inward to the central tendon.
Caval opening
The inferior vena cava passes through an opening in the right side of the central tendon.
Esophageal hiatus
The esophagus passes through a muscular opening behind the central tendon. Fibers mainly from the right crus loop around the opening.
Aortic hiatus
The aorta passes behind the diaphragm between the crura, under the median arcuate ligament. It does not pierce the muscle or tendon.
Right crus
This longer right-hand bundle anchors the diaphragm to the upper lumbar spine. In this view from below, it appears on the left of the image.
